hub_subtitle: Business English para seguros, reuniões e entrevistas — e o desbloqueio da fala, do primeiro dia ao último

lesson.menu_title: What Were You Doing? -- The Past Continuous and the Moment Everything Stopped
lesson.menu_desc: Na aula 17 a Paula aprendeu was e were e contou como as coisas foram. Hoje ela cola um verbo em -ing atrás deles e ganha a habilidade que o trabalho dela exige todo dia: contar o que estava acontecendo no exato momento em que algo deu errado. E o cenário é o mais real possível — um incêndio no armazém 4 de um cliente em Santos, às 6h55 de uma terça-feira. A aula é de LEITURA: ela lê o relatório de ocorrência do gerente do local (doze pessoas trabalhando às 6h40, dois homens carregando um caminhão, ninguém usando a máquina velha) e descobre que quem estava fazendo o quê é o que decide um sinistro. Seis palavras novas (happen, claim, warehouse, fire, damage, suddenly), a estrutura da interrupção (I was writing the report when the client called), e o Greg de Miami pedindo o que ninguêm tinha pedido a ela antes: “me manda a história, não só os números.” -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- What Were You Doing?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Paula Morales | Lesson 18 -- What Were You Doing? (Past Continuous)
lesson.grammar_point: past continuous -- was/were + verb-ing for an action in progress in the past; the interruption pattern with when (I was writing the report when the client called), two actions at the same time with while, the negative (nobody was using the machine) and the question What were you doing...?

listenings.text: Hi, Paula. David here. Greg told me you sent the Santos report, and I want to tell you why he called you about it. Twelve years ago I was working on my first big claim. A fire in a factory, at night. I sent Miami a perfect page. The numbers were correct, the photos were good, and the dates were right. And Miami said no. They did not pay for four months. Four months, Paula. Do you know what was missing? Nobody wrote what the team was doing when the fire started. Nothing. Not one line. So the reinsurer read my page and they asked, was somebody working with fire that night? Was somebody using the old machine? And I could not answer, because I did not ask. The people were there, the answer was there, and I only asked three weeks later. By then, nobody remembered. So here is the thing I learned, and it is the only thing I really want you to keep from this call. In this job, what happened is easy. Anybody can write what happened. What was happening is the hard part, and it is the part that pays the claim.

Good morning, Paula. Sofia here, and I am going to be quick, because I only want to say one thing. This week you did something for the first time, and I do not think you noticed. Greg called you directly about the Santos fire. Not me. You. And you answered him in English, alone, about an international account, at seven in the morning. Two years ago you were sending me the reports and I was talking to Miami. Now you are talking to Miami. That happened this week, and nobody made an announcement. Now, about the grammar you learned today. I want you to see why it is not small. In our job there are two questions, and they are not the same question. What happened? A fire started at six fifty-five. Anybody can find that. But what was happening? Twelve people were working, two men were loading a truck, three women were checking boxes, and nobody was using the old machine. That second answer is the one the reinsurer reads first, and it is the one that decides if the client is paid. It is a small piece of English and it carries an enormous amount of money. So keep asking it, Paula. Every single time. What were you doing when it happened? See you Thursday.

reading.rtitle: Incident Report — Warehouse 4, Santos — Tuesday, 6:55 a.m.
paras: At 6:40 on Tuesday morning, twelve people were working in warehouse 4. Two men were loading a truck at door 2. Three women were checking boxes near the office. Nobody was using the old machine, and nobody was smoking.
At 6:55 the night manager was closing his report in the office when he heard a noise. He was walking to door 3 when the fire started. It started near the old machine, and it was very fast.
The alarm rang and everybody left the building in four minutes. Nobody was hurt. While the team was leaving, one driver was moving his truck away from door 2, and that truck has no damage today.
The fire damaged half of the warehouse. We opened the claim this morning. I will send the photos and the list of the boxes today, and I will answer every question from Miami this week.
reading.source: Ricardo Alves — site manager, Warehouse 4, Santos — first notice of loss

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the incident report?
choices: It is a list of the boxes that warehouse 4 sold last month, with the final numbers.
It is the report of a fire in warehouse 4: what everybody was doing at 6:40, how the fire started at 6:55, that nobody was hurt, and that the claim is now open.
It is an invitation from the site manager to visit warehouse 4 in Santos next week.

items: The fire started at 6:40 in the morning.
f
No. At 6:40 the team was working normally — twelve people. The fire started at 6:55, fifteen minutes later.
The night manager was closing his report when he heard a noise.
t
Yes: "the night manager was closing his report in the office when he heard a noise." He was in the office, not near the machine.
Somebody was using the old machine when the fire started.
f
No. The report says nobody was using the old machine. The fire started near it — but nobody was using it, and that line matters.
One driver was moving his truck away from door 2 while the team was leaving.
t
Yes — two things at the same time. And that is why that truck has no damage today.
Somebody was hurt in the fire.
f
No. The alarm rang, everybody left in four minutes and nobody was hurt. That is the first line Miami looks for.

bank.label: What was happening / O que estava acontecendo
items: What were you doing when it happened?
I was writing the report when the client called.
The team was loading a truck at that moment.
Nobody was using the old machine.
While the team was leaving, a driver was moving his truck.

bank.label: Opening a claim / Abrindo um sinistro
items: We opened the claim this morning.
The fire damaged half of the warehouse.
Nobody was hurt.
Suddenly, everybody stopped and left the building.
I will send the photos today.

items.situation: Greg asks: "What were you doing at 6:40 on Tuesday morning?" Answer with a full sentence.
tips: I was reading my emails at 6:40.
I was driving to the office when Santos called me.

items.situation: Tell Miami what the warehouse team was doing when the fire started.
tips: Two men were loading a truck and three women were checking boxes.
They were working normally, and nobody was using the old machine.

items.situation: A client asks what happened. Give the fact, the time and the damage.
tips: There was a fire at 6:55 on Tuesday morning.
The fire started near the old machine and it damaged half of the warehouse.

items.situation: Use "while" to say that two things were happening at the same time at the warehouse.
tips: While the team was leaving, a driver was moving his truck.
While I was writing the report, Miami was calling the broker.

items.situation: Sofia asks if anybody was hurt. Answer, and say what saved them.
tips: No, nobody was hurt. The alarm rang and everybody left in four minutes.
Nobody was hurt — they were leaving before the fire arrived at door 2.

items.situation: Say what you were doing yesterday at eight in the evening.
tips: I was having dinner at eight.
I was watching the news when my phone rang.
